newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England job vacancies pile up.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England job vacancies pile up.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's second shake-up of the Bank of England in a fortnight means there is yet another top job going, but the government has made no moves to fill the growing list of vacancies.

Shortly after being elected on May 1, the new Labour government made the central bank responsible for setting interest rates and said it would be appointing a second deputy governor to help with this task.
On Tuesday, Brown announced a transfer of the Bank of England's regulatory role to a revamped Securities and Investments Board, and appointed bank deputy governor Howard Davies to head it.
Mervyn King, the central bank's chief economist, is the favourite to replace Howard Davies.
"Mervyn is both ambitious and capable," said one former Bank of England official. "He's missed out on the appointment twice, so maybe it will be third time lucky."

Both Davies and his predecessor, Rupert Pennant-Rea, were appointed over King's head. Until the news of Davies's impending departure, it had been assumed he would miss out a third time in favour of Goldman Sachs economist Gavyn Davies.
When the new chancellor announced two weeks ago he would be appointing a second deputy governor it was assumed that Gavyn Davies, who has long been an adviser of the Labour Party, would get the job.

But so far no announcements have been forthcoming, so the new nine-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is down to three known members, if Howard Davies is excluded. Moreover, King is already widely assumed to be a member in his capacity of executive director for the bank.

The Treasury says it does not know when the MPC members will be announced. Howard Davies' replacement could be announced at any time but the statutes of the central bank say that it has just one deputy and these need to be changed before the second appointment can be made.
Some members of Britain's finance community are beginning to fret at the delay. "It seems odd that they hadn't already sorted out who was going to be on the committee," one ex-Treasury official said.

"They haven't been in office three weeks and they've made the Bank of England independent and stripped it of its regulatory powers. It's a bit strange that they can't sort out who's on the committee," he said.

The membership of the committee will be crucial if the new Labour government, which ousted the 18-year old Conservative administration on May 1, is to maintain the market credibility earned with the transfer of interest rate powers to the central bank.

"If I'm Mr Brown and I'm trying to be radical about who sets monetary policy, it might actually be counter-productive if I were seen to be stacking the committee with my chums," a second ex-bank official warned.
"Gavyn Davies' problem may be that he's very much seen to be a friend of Mr. Brown's," he added.

Mervyn King's other major selling point is the respect in which he is held by the markets. "If anything the danger with Mervyn is that he will be too tough on inflation but that's not necessarily a bad thing in the market's eyes."

Gavyn Davies told Reuters this morning that he did not expect to be approached to become a deputy governor and that he had not been asked thus far. "As to whether I'll be one of them, no-one has said a word to me. I haven't the faintest idea."
But the transferral of the Bank of England's regulatory role to the SIB has left a question-mark over what exactly the second deputy governor will cover.

The official split in responsibilities announced by Brown was that one deputy would support the governor on monetary stability and the other on financial stability -- the second role has been substantially eroded.

Nevertheless, a Treasury official said Brown would still be appointing two deputy governors while Gavyn Davies said "there will still be two wings in the bank -- economics and the inflation control wing."

And at a press conference on Wednesday morning to announce the central bank's annual results, Governor Eddie George was keen to stress that the bank still had a crucial role to play in ensuring financial stability.
